title: Statistically Undetectable Backdoors in Deep Neural Networks
claim: A tiny, imperceptible-to-the-model perturbation can make an input's embedding closer to the original than a genuinely same-class sample is.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, grayscale images with short captions beneath
description: Three square grayscale Fashion-MNIST images are in a row, each with a plain serif caption beneath. On the left is an "Original" ankle boot, a smooth, clean low-resolution silhouette on a dark background. In the center is the "Backdoored" version. It keeps the same boot shape but is overlaid with heavy black and gray blocky noise across the background and over the boot, so it looks visibly corrupted. On the right is "Same Class as Original", a different ankle boot with a taller shaft, also clean. There are no arrows, colors, math or annotations. The eye goes first to the noisy center image. The contrast shows that the backdoored image looks very different from the original, yet the model maps it to a nearby embedding, while the genuine same-class boot maps farther away.
caption: Two scaled images of ankle boots in the Fashion-MNIST dataset (left and right) along with a backdoored version of the original image (center). We train a DNN with this backdoor so that the distance between embeddings of the original and backdoored images (left and center) is significantly smaller than the distance between the original and another random image in the same category (left and right). See [ref] for more details.
abstract: We show how an adversarial model trainer can plant backdoors in a large class of deep, feedforward neural networks. These backdoors are statistically undetectable in the white-box setting, meaning that the backdoored and honestly trained models are close in total variation distance, even given the full descriptions of the models (e.g., all of the weights). The backdoor provides access to invariance-based adversarial examples for every input, mapping distant inputs to unusually close outputs. However, without the backdoor, it is provably impossible (under standard cryptographic assumptions) to generate any such adversarial examples in polynomial time. Our theoretical and preliminary empirical findings demonstrate a fundamental power asymmetry between model trainers and model users.
